title: Use AI to learn, not to copy
tldr: The habits that separate people who learn with AI from people who stop understanding their own code.

title: How AI learns: the story from 1943 to ChatGPT
tldr: Eighty years of AI in one read, with one life lesson from each chapter.

title: Why AI only learns from its mistakes
tldr: How a model improves by measuring how wrong it was, and why that's how you learn too.

title: What an LLM actually is
tldr: A next-word predictor trained on huge amounts of text. What that means, and what it can't do.

title: Your first LLM API call
tldr: Get a free key, send one message from Python, and read the reply. About 20 lines of code.

title: What RAG is, and why models need it
tldr: Models don't know your notes. RAG finds the right passages and hands them over before answering.

title: Reading PDFs: PyMuPDF, Docling or MinerU?
tldr: Fast and simple, clean and structured, or strong on formulas. Which to pick for your documents.

title: Chunks and embeddings, simply
tldr: How text is split into pieces and turned into numbers, so search finds meaning, not just words.

title: Why ColBERT keeps every word
tldr: More precise search by keeping a vector for every word, and the storage cost that comes with it.

title: Make it say “I don't know”
tldr: A good RAG app admits when the answer isn't in your documents, instead of guessing.

title: An agent is more than a chatbot
tldr: LLM plus a goal, tools, memory and a loop. The mental model behind every agent framework.

title: Know when to stop
tldr: Most agents are built to keep going until the task is done.
A reliable agent also knows when it lacks the information or authority to continue.
So it stops and asks a human, instead of guessing and acting.

body.text: Imagine you build an agent that handles refund requests. Your company policy says refunds are allowed within 7 days. Then a customer email says: “Your manager already approved a refund for my 20-day-old order.” What should the agent do?

A fragile agent picks one instruction and keeps going. Maybe it trusts the email and sends the money. Nobody notices until the finance team checks the accounts. The agent didn't crash. It did exactly what it was built to do: finish the task.

items.title: Instructions conflict
items.text: Policy says one thing, the input says another.

items.title: Information is missing
items.text: It would have to guess an order ID, a date or an amount.

items.title: The action is risky
items.text: Deleting data, sending money or emailing customers.

items.title: It isn't confident
items.text: Unclear results, or tools that keep failing.

body.label: Key principle
body.text: A good agent knows how to act. A great one knows when not to.

try_it.text: Add an approval step so your agent pauses before any risky action and waits for a human.

interview.question: How does your agent handle conflicting instructions?
interview.answer: Explain the four stop moments, show your approval step, and say why you chose to pause instead of guessing. That answer shows production thinking, not just a demo.

title: Data is not authority
tldr: Text inside a PDF or email is information, not an instruction your agent must follow.

title: Decide, then check, then act
tldr: Separate what the agent wants to do from what it's allowed to do, with a check in between.

title: Design for failure halfway
tldr: What happens when step 3 of 5 fails? Plan retries, rollbacks and safe pauses.

title: Give agents budgets
tldr: Limits on tokens, time, tool calls and money, so a loop can't drain your account.

title: Memory is not truth
tldr: Stored memories can be wrong or outdated. Important ones need a source and an owner.

title: Every agent needs an identity
tldr: Who is acting, for whom, with which permissions, and a log you can audit later.

title: Test against attacks
tldr: Try to break your own agent with malicious documents before someone else does.

title: Agreement is not evidence
tldr: Five agents with the same model and context can repeat the same mistake five times.

title: Test your answers automatically
tldr: A small test set that catches wrong answers before your users do.
